title: C.R.E.A.M. and the Charmels
hook: C.R.E.A.M. is really a 1967 Charmels record.
voiceover: C.R.E.A.M. is really a 1967 Charmels record. The Charmels were a Stax group out of Memphis. In 1967 they cut a single on Volt called As Long As I've Got You, written by Isaac Hayes and David Porter. It wasn't a hit. 26 years later RZA pulled the piano from the intro, looped it, and laid it under Raekwon and Inspectah Deck. That's the whole record. No chorus melody, just that piano rolling over the drums. What changed is the context. A forgotten Memphis soul intro became the sound of Staten Island in 1993. Save this, then go pull the original and hear what RZA left out. What flip should I break down Thursday?
caption: Day 1. The record behind the record, every day, from behind the decks. C.R.E.A.M. (Wu-Tang Clan, Loud, 1993) sits on the piano intro of As Long As I've Got You by The Charmels (Volt, 1967), written by Isaac Hayes and David Porter. RZA kept the piano, changed the world around it. Save this before you go pull the original. Which flip do you want Thursday? 🎹

title: The Amen break lineage
hook: 4 bars of drums. Thousands of records. Nobody got paid.
voiceover: 4 bars of drums. Thousands of records. Nobody got paid. 1969, a Washington DC soul group called The Winstons cut a B-side, Amen, Brother. Halfway through, drummer Gregory Coleman plays 4 bars alone. That's the Amen break. It got pressed onto Ultimate Breaks and Beats, then N.W.A. ran it under Straight Outta Compton in 1988. Then UK producers chopped it into jungle and drum and bass, and it became the fastest moving drum pattern on earth. The Winstons never saw a royalty. In 2015 fans raised over 24,000 pounds for singer Richard Spencer, the first money that break ever sent home. Name a record on the Amen I missed.
caption: The Amen break: Amen, Brother by The Winstons (Metromedia, 1969), drums by Gregory Coleman. Straight Outta Compton, half of jungle, Oasis, and thousands more sit on those 4 bars. The band was never paid for a single sample; a 2015 crowdfund finally sent Richard Spencer some money. I still cut this in drum and bass rooms. Name a record on the Amen I missed and I'll pin the best one. 🥁

title: Amapiano to boom bap staircase
hook: Amapiano to 90s rap without emptying the floor.
voiceover: Amapiano to 90s rap without emptying the floor. Here's the problem. Amapiano sits around 112 BPM. A 90s boom bap record sits around 90. Jump straight across and the room feels the brakes. What I actually do is a 3 record staircase. Out of the amapiano record I go into an afrobeats record around 105, same swing, same log drum feel. From there into a dancehall or reggaeton record around 98. Now the room is already moving at hip-hop pace, so I drop the 90s record at 92 and nobody notices the gear change. 3 records, about 6 minutes, 20 BPM covered. What's your bridge out of amapiano? Drop the BPM.
caption: The transition I get asked about most. Amapiano (around 112) into 90s rap (around 90) is a 20 BPM drop, and if you take it in one jump the floor feels it. My fix is a 3 record staircase: afrobeats at 105, dancehall or reggaeton at 98, then the boom bap record. DJs: what's your bridge out of amapiano? Drop the BPM you land on.

title: The World Is Yours / Ahmad Jamal
hook: The World Is Yours started as Ahmad Jamal, 1970.
voiceover: The World Is Yours started as Ahmad Jamal, 1970. Ahmad Jamal is a Pittsburgh jazz pianist. In 1970 he put out an album on Impulse called The Awakening. Track 2 is I Love Music. A couple of minutes in there's a piano figure that just floats. 24 years later Pete Rock took that figure for Nas on Illmatic. He didn't loop the whole phrase. He grabbed the chords, ran them under his own drums and bassline, and sang the hook himself. Whose world is this. Same piano, different life, and Ahmad Jamal was still touring while it played on every corner. Save this before you go pull The Awakening. Which flip do you want Monday?
caption: The World Is Yours (Nas, Illmatic, Columbia, 1994, produced by Pete Rock) is built on I Love Music from Ahmad Jamal's The Awakening (Impulse!, 1970). Pete Rock took the piano chords, put his own drums under them, and sang the hook himself. The Awakening is one of the most sampled jazz records of the 70s; this is the flip that made me buy it. Which one should I break down Monday?

title: Ultimate Breaks and Beats
hook: Every DJ you respect owned these 25 records.
voiceover: Every DJ you respect owned these 25 records. Ultimate Breaks and Beats. Street Beat Records, New York, 1986 to 1991, put together by Lenny Roberts and Breakbeat Lou. 25 volumes, catalog numbers SB-501 to SB-525. Each one is a compilation of the drum breaks DJs were cutting in the parks. Impeach the President, Apache, Funky Drummer, Amen, Brother, pressed loud on 1 record so you didn't have to carry the originals. Producers sampled straight off these, which is why so many 80s and 90s records share the same drums. Look for the cartoon cover art and the SB number on the label. Send this to the one friend who still buys vinyl.
caption: Crate Notes, week 1. Ultimate Breaks and Beats (Street Beat Records, 1986 to 1991), 25 volumes, SB-501 to SB-525, compiled by Lenny Roberts and Breakbeat Lou. The breaks DJs were cutting in the Bronx parks, pressed onto one record each. Half the drums on golden era rap were sampled straight off these. If you see the cartoon covers in a bin, buy them. Which volume do you own? 📦

title: Don't open with the banger
hook: Your first record shouldn't be a banger. Here's why.
voiceover: Your first record shouldn't be a banger. Here's why. Saturday, doors at 10, I'm on at 10. The room is 12 people and a bartender. If I open with the biggest record I own, I've told those 12 people the peak already happened and they missed it. What I actually do is open around 95 BPM with a record people know but nobody dances to on purpose. It sets the volume, lets the sound guy hear the system, and tells the people walking in that something is coming. I save the first real record for when there's a line at the bar. That's the room telling me it's ready. What do you open with?
caption: Saturday set building. The opening record has one job: tell the room something is coming without spending it. I open around 95 BPM with something familiar that nobody dances to on purpose, let the system settle, and hold the first real record until there's a line at the bar. The room tells you when it's ready if you're watching. DJs, what's your opener tonight?

title: Low End Theory at 35
hook: 35 years ago this month, Low End Theory dropped.
voiceover: 35 years ago this month, Low End Theory dropped. September 24, 1991, A Tribe Called Quest, Jive Records. Everyone posts the green and red cover. Here's the part the pages skip. On Verses from the Abstract, that upright bass is not a sample. It's Ron Carter, the jazz bassist who played with Miles Davis, in the studio, playing live. Carter has said he agreed on 1 condition, no profanity on his track, and Q-Tip kept his word. The rest of the album is jazz records cut by a DJ's ear, Minnie Riperton under Check the Rhime, Art Blakey under Excursions. A rap album that treated jazz like a crate, not a costume. Where were you when this dropped?
caption: The Low End Theory, A Tribe Called Quest, Jive, September 24, 1991. 35 years. The detail that matters: Ron Carter, who played bass with Miles Davis, played live on Verses from the Abstract and, by his own account, asked for no profanity on his track. Elsewhere it's Minnie Riperton under Check the Rhime and Art Blakey under Excursions. Where were you when this dropped?

title: G Thang and Leon Haywood
hook: G Thang is a 1975 Leon Haywood slow jam.
voiceover: G Thang is a 1975 Leon Haywood slow jam. Leon Haywood, born in Houston, working out of Los Angeles. In 1975 he put out I Want'a Do Something Freaky to You on 20th Century Records. It's a bedroom record, and the intro is that bass line and the guitar sting every head knows. In 1992 Dr. Dre took that intro, kept it close to the original tempo, and built Nuthin' but a G Thang on top of it for The Chronic. Snoop's first verse sits right where Leon's vocal used to. The flip isn't a chop. It's a lift, with new drums and that whining synth on top. Save this, then go pull the Haywood and hear how much Dre kept.
caption: Nuthin' but a G Thang (Dr. Dre and Snoop, The Chronic, Death Row, 1992) is built on the intro of I Want'a Do Something Freaky to You by Leon Haywood (20th Century, 1975). Dre barely chopped it. He lifted the groove, added drums and the synth lead, and let Snoop sit where Leon's vocal used to be. The best flips are sometimes the least clever ones. Which West Coast flip next? ☀️
cover_text: G Thang is a 1975 slow jam

title: Apache from Herc to Missy
hook: The bongo break Kool Herc built the Bronx on.
voiceover: The bongo break Kool Herc built the Bronx on. Apache. Written by Jerry Lordan, a 1960 hit for The Shadows in the UK. Then in 1973 Michael Viner's Incredible Bongo Band cut a version in Vancouver, session drummer Jim Gordon on kit, King Errisson on bongos, and partway through the band drops out and it's just drums and bongos. Herc looped that with 2 copies at parties in the Bronx and called it the national anthem of hip-hop. Sugarhill Gang rapped over it in 1981. Nas, Made You Look, 2002. Missy Elliott, We Run This, 2006. I play the Nas and the Missy back to back and the room never clocks it's the same drums. Name a record on Apache I missed.
caption: Apache. Jerry Lordan wrote it, The Shadows had the UK hit in 1960, and in 1973 the Incredible Bongo Band (Michael Viner, Jim Gordon on drums, King Errisson on bongos) cut the version Kool Herc built the Bronx on. Sugarhill Gang, Nas's Made You Look, Missy's We Run This, and hundreds more sit on that break. Still my favourite drums to cut at 2am. Name a record on Apache I missed.

title: The break cue point
hook: 1 cue point that makes 90s rap mix cleaner.
voiceover: 1 cue point that makes 90s rap mix cleaner. Most 90s rap records were built on a drum loop. Before the first verse, or between verses, there's usually a stretch where it's just the loop, no vocals. I set a cue point right at the top of that stretch on every record I carry. Call it the break cue. When I'm mixing out of amapiano or club and the incoming rap record needs to sit for a while, I jump to the break cue, let the loop ride under the outgoing record for 16 bars, and the room hears drums, not a verse fighting a verse. It takes 20 seconds a record during prep. What's your prep routine?
caption: Midweek prep tip. Every 90s rap record has a stretch where it's just the loop and no vocals. I put a cue point at the top of it on every track I carry, the break cue, so when I'm coming out of amapiano or jersey club I can ride 16 bars of drums instead of a verse fighting a verse. 20 seconds per record in prep, hours of clean blends. What's your prep routine?

title: Through the Wire / Chaka Khan
hook: Kanye sped Chaka Khan up and made a career.
voiceover: Kanye sped Chaka Khan up and made a career. 1984, Chaka Khan releases Through the Fire on Warner Bros, written by David Foster, Tom Keane and Cynthia Weil. A power ballad. October 2002, Kanye is in a car accident in Los Angeles, jaw wired shut. About 2 weeks later he records Through the Wire with his mouth still wired. The beat is Chaka's chorus pitched up until she sounds like a cartoon, the chipmunk soul thing he'd already done for Jay-Z. The tempo jumps from ballad to head nod. What changed is the pitch and the meaning. Through the fire became through the wire, and the sample is the punchline. Save this, and tell me which Kanye flip you want next.
caption: Through the Wire (Kanye West, The College Dropout, Roc-A-Fella, 2004) is Chaka Khan's Through the Fire (Warner Bros, 1984, written by David Foster, Tom Keane and Cynthia Weil) pitched up. He recorded it with his jaw wired shut about 2 weeks after the October 2002 crash. The sample is the punchline. Which Kanye flip should I break down next? 🔥

title: Bob James One
hook: Nautilus lives on a 1974 record under 20 dollars.
voiceover: Nautilus lives on a 1974 record under 20 dollars. Bob James, One, CTI Records, 1974. Last track on side 2 is Nautilus. That bass and electric piano is under Ghostface's Daytona 500, Slick Rick's Children's Story, Run-DMC's Beats to the Rhyme, and that's a short list. CTI pressed a lot of these, so originals turn up everywhere for less than a takeout order. What to look for. The gatefold with the CTI logo, and check the run-out groove for the Van Gelder stamp, because Rudy Van Gelder mastered most of that catalog and those copies play loud. Send this to the friend who still buys vinyl. What's the record you'd never sell?
caption: Bob James, One (CTI, 1974). The last track, Nautilus, is under Ghostface's Daytona 500, Slick Rick's Children's Story, Run-DMC's Beats to the Rhyme and a long list after that. CTI pressed plenty, so this is a common record with an uncommon amount of rap history inside it. Look for the gatefold and the Van Gelder stamp in the dead wax. What's the record you'd never sell? 🎧

title: The 1:55am record
hook: The record that clears the bar at 1:55am.
voiceover: The record that clears the bar at 1:55am. Every room has one. Not the biggest record of the night, the one that pulls people off the bar stools onto the floor with drinks still in their hands. In my rooms it's usually a 2000s record everybody knows the words to, played 20 minutes before close, not at close. Here's the move. I don't mix into it. I cut the outgoing record dead on the 1, half a second of silence, then the intro. Silence is the loudest thing a DJ has. The room turns to look and the first bar does the rest. What's your 1:55am record? Drop it and where you play.
caption: Saturday night craft. Every room has a record that clears the bar at 1:55am, and it's rarely the biggest record you own. It's the one everybody knows the words to, played 20 minutes before close. I don't mix into it. I cut dead on the 1, half a second of silence, then the intro. Silence is the loudest thing a DJ has. What's your 1:55am record, and where do you play?

title: Ready to Die at 32
hook: 32 years ago this month, Ready to Die dropped.
voiceover: 32 years ago this month, Ready to Die dropped. September 13, 1994, Bad Boy Records. Everyone posts the baby on the cover. The part nobody posts is the intro, and it's a DJ set. The first 3 minutes of the album tell Big's life through records. He's born to Curtis Mayfield's Superfly. He's a kid to Rapper's Delight. He's a teenager robbing a train to Audio Two's Top Billin'. He walks out of prison to Snoop's Tha Shiznit, which had only been out about 10 months. Puffy scored a biography with 4 records and no narration, and every head in Brooklyn knew exactly what year each scene was. Where were you when this dropped?
caption: Ready to Die, The Notorious B.I.G., Bad Boy, September 13, 1994. 32 years. The intro is a DJ set of his life: Superfly for the birth, Rapper's Delight for childhood, Top Billin' for the train robbery, Tha Shiznit for walking out of prison. Four records, no narration, and you knew the year of every scene. Where were you when this dropped? 🗽

title: Paid in Full, 3 continents
hook: Paid in Full borrows its bassline from a Temptation.
voiceover: Paid in Full borrows its bassline from a Temptation. Dennis Edwards sang lead for the Temptations. In 1984 he went solo with Don't Look Any Further on Gordy, a duet with Siedah Garrett, and that bassline is the whole hook of the record. 1987, Eric B and Rakim take the bassline and put the drums from the Soul Searchers' Ashley's Roachclip underneath it. Then Coldcut remix it in London and drop in Ofra Haza, an Israeli singer, performing Im Nin'alu, a Yemenite Jewish poem, over the top. The Seven Minutes of Madness mix went top 20 in the UK. Detroit, Washington, Tel Aviv and London on 1 record in 1987. Save this. Which flip next?
caption: Paid in Full (Eric B and Rakim, 4th and Broadway, 1987). Bassline from Dennis Edwards' Don't Look Any Further (Gordy, 1984), drums from the Soul Searchers' Ashley's Roachclip (1974), and in Coldcut's Seven Minutes of Madness remix, Ofra Haza's Im Nin'alu, a Yemenite Jewish poem, on top. Four cities, one record, before anyone was clearing samples. Which flip do you want Thursday?

title: Funky Drummer and Clyde Stubblefield
hook: 20 seconds of drums. No credit on the sleeve.
voiceover: 20 seconds of drums. No credit on the sleeve. November 1969, King Studios, Cincinnati. James Brown's band is cutting Funky Drummer. Late in the take, Brown tells everybody to lay out and lets Clyde Stubblefield play 8 bars alone. That's the break. Released in 1970 as a 2 part single, and Stubblefield's name isn't on it. Fight the Power. Mama Said Knock You Out. Run's House. George Michael's Waiting for That Day. Hundreds more. Stubblefield said in interviews he never got a royalty for any of it, because the record belonged to James Brown, not the drummer. I still cut those 8 bars in every hip-hop room I play. Name a record on Funky Drummer I missed.
caption: Funky Drummer, James Brown, recorded November 1969 at King Studios in Cincinnati, released 1970. The 8 bars Clyde Stubblefield plays alone are under Fight the Power, Mama Said Knock You Out, Run's House, George Michael, Sinead O'Connor and hundreds more. Stubblefield wasn't credited and, by his own account, never saw a royalty. Name a record on Funky Drummer I missed. 🥁

title: Gain staging for club rooms
hook: Red on the master, and the room hears amateur.
voiceover: Red on the master, and the room hears amateur. Nobody on the floor knows what a limiter is. They just feel that the hi-hats turned to sand and the log drum stopped hitting. That's clipping. What I actually do. Channel gains set so the loudest part of each record peaks around minus 6 on the channel meter, master at 0 and left alone all night. If the room needs to be louder, that's the sound guy's amp, not my master. When I bring a 2020s record mastered hot in next to a 1994 record mastered quiet, I fix it on the channel trim before it's live, not on the fader. What do you set your channels at?
caption: Midweek craft. Clipping doesn't sound like distortion to a crowd, it sounds like the DJ is bad. My rule: channel gains so each record peaks around minus 6, master at 0 and untouched all night, and volume is the sound engineer's job. Modern records are mastered much hotter than 90s records, so match them on the trim before they're live. DJs, where do you set your channels?

title: Shook Ones hidden piano
hook: Shook Ones hid a Herbie Hancock piano for 16 years.
voiceover: Shook Ones hid a Herbie Hancock piano for 16 years. 1995, Havoc builds Shook Ones Part 2 for The Infamous. That eerie loop, the one that sounds like a kettle about to go, everybody assumed was a keyboard. Nobody could name it. Then around 2011 heads on the sampling forums matched it. It's Herbie Hancock, Jessica, from the 1969 Fat Albert Rotunda album on Warner Bros. Havoc took a couple of seconds of piano, pitched it up hard, and chopped it until the notes stopped sounding like piano. That's why it hid, and Havoc later confirmed it. The lesson for producers, pitch and chop until your own mother wouldn't recognise it. Save this and go hear Jessica.
caption: Shook Ones Part II (Mobb Deep, The Infamous, Loud, 1995, produced by Havoc). For 16 years nobody could name the loop. It's Jessica, from Herbie Hancock's Fat Albert Rotunda (Warner Bros, 1969), pitched up and chopped until the piano stopped sounding like a piano. Identified by sample hunters around 2011, later confirmed by Havoc. What should I break down Monday?

title: Hot Buttered Soul
hook: If you own 1 Isaac Hayes record, it's this.
voiceover: If you own 1 Isaac Hayes record, it's this. Hot Buttered Soul, Enterprise Records, a Stax label, 1969. 4 songs on the whole album. Walk On By runs 12 minutes and the guitar and strings in the first minute are under Biggie's Warning. Hyperbolicsyllabicsesquedalymistic is the piano and drums under Public Enemy's Black Steel in the Hour of Chaos. 2 of the biggest records of 2 decades off 1 album. What to look for. The bald head on the cover, the Enterprise label, and catalog number ENS-1001. Then check that side 2 plays clean, because By the Time I Get to Phoenix is 18 minutes and the last inch of a worn copy is trouble. Send this to the friend who still buys vinyl.
caption: Hot Buttered Soul, Isaac Hayes, Enterprise ENS-1001, 1969. Four songs. Walk On By is under Biggie's Warning, Hyperbolicsyllabicsesquedalymistic is under Public Enemy's Black Steel in the Hour of Chaos, and that's before you get to the 18 minute Phoenix on side 2. The record that proved soul albums could be long. What's the record you'd never sell? 🎙️

title: Rap vocal, jersey club drums
hook: Turning a rap acapella into a jersey club moment.
voiceover: Turning a rap acapella into a jersey club moment. Jersey club lives at 130 to 140 BPM. A 90s rap record lives around 90. You can't beatmatch those. What I actually do. I bring up a club track with a long drum intro, that Think break kick pattern everybody in Newark grew up on, and I drop the rap vocal over it for 1 line only, as a shout. Not a blend, a tease. The room hears a line they know over drums they're already dancing to, they scream, and the vocal's gone. Then I play the actual jersey flip of that record, the one the Jersey producers already made. Tease, then payoff. What rap line gets the biggest scream in your room?
caption: Saturday craft. You can't beatmatch a 90 BPM rap record into jersey club at 135, so don't try. Drop one line of the vocal as a shout over the club drums, let the room scream, pull it, then play the jersey flip of that record the Newark producers already made. Tease, then payoff. DJs, what rap line gets the biggest scream in your room?

title: Food and Liquor at 20
hook: 20 years ago this month, Food and Liquor dropped.
voiceover: 20 years ago this month, Food and Liquor dropped. September 19, 2006, Lupe Fiasco, 1st and 15th and Atlantic. Everyone posts the skateboard. The part nobody posts is where Kick, Push comes from. Producer Soundtrakk built it on Bolero Medley, a 1979 record by Celeste Legaspi, a singer from the Philippines. Those strings and that rising vocal line are Manila, not Chicago. So the biggest skateboard record in rap is a Filipino ballad from the 70s, chopped and looped, which sums up the whole album, a West Side Chicago kid pulling from everywhere. Ask your Filipino friends, their parents know that record. Where were you when this dropped?
caption: Lupe Fiasco's Food and Liquor, 1st and 15th / Atlantic, September 19, 2006. 20 years. Kick, Push, produced by Soundtrakk, is built on Bolero Medley by Celeste Legaspi (1979), a Filipino singer. Chicago rap on a Manila ballad, and somehow it's the most skateboard record ever made. Where were you when this dropped? 🛹

title: Ms. Jackson backwards guitar
hook: Ms. Jackson is built on Strawberry Letter 23.
voiceover: Ms. Jackson is built on Strawberry Letter 23. 1977, the Brothers Johnson, produced by Quincy Jones, cut Strawberry Letter 23 for A&M. It's a Shuggie Otis song from 1971, but the Johnsons made it a hit, and the guitar figure near the end is the famous part. In 2000 Earthtone 3, that's Andre 3000, Big Boi and David Sheats, took that guitar and turned it around under Ms. Jackson. Not the loop you'd expect. It's reversed, played backwards, so the guitar seems to breathe in instead of out. That's why the record feels like an apology. Stankonia, LaFace, and it went number 1 in early 2001. Save this, then go hear the guitar the right way round.
caption: Ms. Jackson (OutKast, Stankonia, LaFace, 2000, produced by Earthtone III) is the guitar from Strawberry Letter 23 by the Brothers Johnson (A&M, 1977, produced by Quincy Jones), a Shuggie Otis song from 1971, played backwards. The reversal is why it sounds like an apology. Went number 1 in February 2001. Which Southern flip should I break down next? 🍑

title: Impeach the President
hook: Queens teenagers cut the drums under golden era rap.
voiceover: Queens teenagers cut the drums under golden era rap. 1973. A soul singer named Roy C. Hammond has a small label, Alaga Records. He produces a group of high school kids from Jamaica, Queens, called The Honey Drippers, on a protest record about Nixon, Impeach the President. The record didn't sell. The first 2 bars did. Marley Marl put those drums under MC Shan's The Bridge in 1986. Audio Two, Top Billin'. Nice and Smooth, Funky for You. LL Cool J, Around the Way Girl. Janet Jackson, That's the Way Love Goes. Hundreds more, from the Bronx to Minneapolis. The kids were never famous. Their drummer is on more records than most drummers alive. Name a record on Impeach I missed.
caption: Impeach the President, The Honey Drippers, Alaga Records, 1973, produced by Roy C. Hammond with a band of high school kids from Jamaica, Queens. The record sank; the first two bars of drums are under The Bridge, Top Billin', Funky for You, Around the Way Girl, Janet's That's the Way Love Goes and hundreds more. Name a record on Impeach I missed and I'll pin the best one.

title: When key mixing actually matters
hook: Key mixing is overrated, except in these 3 spots.
voiceover: Key mixing is overrated, except in these 3 spots. Most of the night I don't look at the key. Drums are drums, and a clean 8 bar blend on the beat is fine. But 3 places I check. 1, amapiano. Those records have a long melodic intro and a long melodic outro, so a blend runs 32 bars and a clash of keys sits there for a full minute. 2, any time I'm laying a vocal or an acapella over another record, wrong key and the singer sounds seasick. 3, the last 2 records of the night, because they're the ones people walk home humming. Everything else, mix on the drums and trust your ears. When do you check the key?
caption: Midweek craft. I don't key mix most of the night, drums are drums. I check in 3 places: amapiano blends, because the melodic intros and outros overlap for 32 bars; vocals or acapellas over another record; and the last 2 records, the ones people hum walking home. Everything else, ears over software. DJs, when do you actually check the key?

title: Nice for What, 4 generations
hook: Nice for What is Lauryn Hill sped up.
voiceover: Nice for What is Lauryn Hill sped up. 1998, The Miseducation, Ex-Factor, the line, care for me, care for me. 2018, Murda Beatz takes that line, pitches it up, and sets it over New Orleans bounce drums with Big Freedia's voice in the mix. Drake's biggest bounce record. Here's the lineage nobody posts. Ex-Factor itself is built on Wu-Tang's Can It Be All So Simple from 1993, which is built on Gladys Knight singing The Way We Were, Try to Remember, from 1974. So Nice for What is a 4 generation record. Gladys to RZA to Lauryn to Murda Beatz, 44 years, and a DJ can play all 4 in 1 night if the room is right. Save this. What flip next?
caption: Nice for What (Drake, 2018, produced by Murda Beatz, with Big Freedia) is Lauryn Hill's Ex-Factor (1998) sped up over New Orleans bounce. Ex-Factor is built on Wu-Tang's Can It Be All So Simple (1993), which is built on Gladys Knight's The Way We Were / Try to Remember (1974). Four generations, 44 years, one line. Which modern flip should I trace next?

title: Everybody Loves the Sunshine
hook: If you only own 1 Roy Ayers, it's this.
voiceover: If you only own 1 Roy Ayers, it's this. Roy Ayers Ubiquity, Everybody Loves the Sunshine, Polydor, 1976. The title track is the record. Vibes, a synth pad that sounds like heat coming off a road, and that chorus. Mary J. Blige's My Life is built on it, and that's just the most famous one. It's also the record I play at the end of every outdoor set in summer, because nobody has ever walked away from it. What to look for. The original Polydor pressing with Roy's face on the cover, and check the title track for surface noise, because that quiet intro shows every scratch. Send this to the friend who still buys vinyl. What's your summer closer?
caption: Roy Ayers Ubiquity, Everybody Loves the Sunshine, Polydor, 1976. The title track is under Mary J. Blige's My Life and a long list after it, and it's the record I close every outdoor summer set with. Buy the original Polydor for the crate, and check the quiet intro for surface noise before you pay. Send this to the friend who still buys vinyl. What's your summer closer? ☀️

title: The 30 record Saturday bag
hook: 30 records. That's my whole Saturday bag.
voiceover: 30 records. That's my whole Saturday bag. I carry 10,000 tracks on the drive. I play from 30. Here's how the folder gets built. Sunday morning after a gig, before I sleep, I write down every record that moved the room and every one that didn't. The ones that worked go into next Saturday's folder. Roughly 10 hip-hop, 10 amapiano, 10 club. Then during the week I swap 5 of them out for something new, so the set never repeats and I never play a whole night of records I haven't tested. The other 9,970 are for requests and emergencies. Discipline beats a big library. How many records do you actually play in a set?
caption: Saturday set building. 10,000 tracks on the drive, 30 in the folder. Sunday morning I write down what moved the room and what didn't, the winners go into next week's folder, and 5 get swapped for something new midweek so the set never repeats and never goes untested. Everything else is for requests. DJs, how many records do you actually play in a night?

title: 93 til Infinity at 33
hook: 33 years ago this month, 93 'til Infinity dropped.
voiceover: 33 years ago this month, 93 'til Infinity dropped. September 28, 1993, Souls of Mischief, Jive Records, out of Oakland. 4 MCs, all around 18 and 19 years old. Everyone posts the title track. Nobody posts where the beat comes from. A-Plus built it on Heather, a Billy Cobham record from 1974 on the Crosswinds album, Atlantic. Cobham was a jazz fusion drummer, but the part A-Plus took is the electric piano and the soft chords, not the drums. He looped those and put his own drums under them. That's why the record feels like a warm afternoon. A drummer's record with the drums taken out. Where were you when this dropped?
caption: 93 'til Infinity, Souls of Mischief, Jive, September 28, 1993. 33 years. Four Oakland teenagers and a beat by A-Plus built on Heather from Billy Cobham's Crosswinds (Atlantic, 1974), the chords from a jazz fusion drummer's record with his drums left out. Still the sound of a warm afternoon. Where were you when this dropped? 🌉

title: Hard Knock Life and Annie
hook: Hard Knock Life is a Broadway orphan chorus.
voiceover: Hard Knock Life is a Broadway orphan chorus. 1977, the musical Annie opens on Broadway. Charles Strouse and Martin Charnin write It's the Hard-Knock Life, a stage full of orphan kids scrubbing floors and singing about it. 1998, New Jersey's DJ Mark the 45 King takes the kids' chorus from the original cast recording, keeps it almost untouched, and puts a hard drum pattern under it. title: Think, from JBs to jersey club
hook: Lyn Collins' Think is under every jersey club set.
voiceover: Lyn Collins' Think is under every jersey club set. 1972, Lyn Collins, the Female Preacher, records Think About It, written and produced by James Brown, on People Records, with the JBs as the band. Midway through, the drums drop to just kick and snare and there's that Yeah, Woo shout. 1988, Rob Base and DJ E-Z Rock loop it and It Takes Two happens. Then club music takes it. Baltimore and Newark DJs in the 90s built their whole kick pattern around the Think break, sped up past 130, and jersey club still runs on those drums and that shout today. So when I go from a 90s rap record into a jersey record, sometimes it's the same drums 20 years apart. Name a record on Think I missed.
caption: Think (About It), Lyn Collins, People Records, 1972, written and produced by James Brown with the JBs. The break and the Yeah, Woo shout are under It Takes Two (1988) and, sped up past 130, under the whole of Baltimore and jersey club. It's the bridge between the two rooms I play most. Name a record on Think I missed and I'll pin the best answer. 🔊
